reason: Both lists stay in the brutal/technical death metal zone the seed occupies. a_recs pairs one Aborted cut with Cattle Decapitation, Hate Eternal and Origin — all sharing the blasting, technical, gore-tinged attack; only Unleashed's old-school Swedish chug sits a bit apart. b_recs is mostly Aborted's own catalogue, which fits sonically but adds little a listener wouldn't already have, and the short 'Interlude' is filler rather than a song. I cannot place I-Zax's sound — I don't know this Thai act's genre, era or production character well enough to judge whether the candidates match, and guessing from the song title or the surrounding Thai rock names would not be a real judgement.

Better spread, no misfire.

tokiwa sits in the Japanese kawaii future bass / doujin electronic world. a_recs lands squarely there: the Aiobahn remix and Such share the same sugary synth-and-vocal production, and the tokiwa track is a natural continuation, with a couple of obscure names I can't place. b_recs scatters across UK trance, 90s Eurodance and J-pop vocal work with no shared production character or scene, so it reads as a generic electronic grab bag rather than a 'more like this' result.

I cannot place "Hinterland (Rabbit Hole)" by Koa; the surrounding candidates point ambiguously toward either the brony/pony music scene or the internet anime-cover space, and I do not know this artist's actual sound well enough to judge which recommendations match its genre, tempo or production character. The seed is a Spanish-language anime-theme cover with polished pop-vocal production. The Big Hash sits in the South African trap/emo-rap lane, and b_recs stays right in that scene: FLVME is essentially the same sonic world, Maraza close by, with K.O and Fifi Cooper broader SA hip-hop but still plausible. a_recs drifts to UK neo-soul and American indie folk (Olivia Dean, Wye Oak), which share nothing with the seed's autotuned trap production, and the remaining picks I can't place. b_recs is the more useful list despite leaning on the seed artist for one slot.

The seed is dissonant, hypnotic avant-garde black metal with industrial-tinged repetition. a_recs stays squarely in that world: The Ruins of Beverast and Misþyrming for dissonant atmosphere, Akhlys for ritual menace, Drudkh for tremolo-driven melancholy, plus a fitting Blut aus Nord cut. b_recs offers metalcore, rap metal and electronica/soundtrack material with no tie to the seed's genre, era or production character.

a_recs is five more Jean Ritchie traditionals - all perfectly in keeping with her unaccompanied/dulcimer Appalachian style, but a listener who just played her already has these, and nothing is opened up. b_recs keeps the same old-time and folk-revival world - Elizabeth Cotten, the Kossoy Sisters' Appalachian harmony, Roscoe Holcomb's Kentucky high-lonesome - while reaching across the scene; Henry Thomas is a more distant pre-war songster, and one Ritchie track anchors it.

Energy Flash is a 1990 hard rave/techno landmark. a_recs stays inside that world: Mentasm is its sibling hoover-riff anthem, Outlander's Vamp is the Belgian rave counterpart, and Dave Clarke, Substance and Dave Angel are all early-90s techno of the same relentless, stripped, dark character. b_recs wanders into melodic deep house, contemporary jazz, indie psych and 2000s electro house — only Benassi is even dance music, and its bouncy electro has nothing to do with the seed's raw rave attack.

A is five more Krallice tracks — all sonically right, dissonant riff-driven avant black metal with the same bass-forward production, but a listener who just played a Krallice deep cut gains almost nothing from a list of Krallice deep cuts. B is the more useful result.

I cannot reliably place this seed: the name 'Iron Mind' and the title could belong either to a metallic hardcore band or to an industrial/electronic project, and the two candidate lists point in opposite directions (modern hardcore bands versus remix-suffixed electronic tracks). 周云蓬's 九月 is spare poetic Chinese folk with a weathered baritone. Overall b delivers a more reliably fitting and better-rounded set.

Both lists stay inside the French frenchcore/tribecore world, so fit is broadly comparable. a_recs keeps one SKRY track for continuity and otherwise reaches across the same scene — Farfacid, Von Bikräv, Fasotek, Vortek's all share the kicks, distorted rave stabs and tempo range. b_recs is five more SKRY cuts: they fit, but a listener who just played SKRY gains little from a catalogue dump. The seed is a gentle mid-2000s Mandopop piano/acoustic ballad. a_recs stays squarely in that lane: Joi Chua's own companion ballad, Maggie Chiang and Hou Xiangting's soft female ballads of the same era, plus adjacent male ballads. b_recs has one strong same-artist ballad, but Daniel Chan and Bibi Zhou sit in different pop registers, and two picks are obscure enough that the list feels scattershot rather than a coherent 'more like this'.

Shin Yong Jae's territory is emotive Korean ballads and drama OSTs. Tan Dun's theme music sits in the lyrical cinematic-orchestral world of solo strings plus Chinese colour. a_recs lands that squarely with the Crouching Tiger theme and Yo-Yo Ma's Memoirs of a Geisha cue, and stays at least within solo-string classical elsewhere, though the Sarasate and Ysaye pieces are virtuoso concert repertoire rather than film scoring. b_recs offers Chinese hip-hop/pop tracks with no orchestral or scoring connection, plus several tracks I cannot place, making it far weaker as a 'more like this' result.

The seed is raw 1980 Japanese rock'n'roll with Kiyoshiro's ragged vocal. b_recs stays in that world: another RC single from the same period, Sheena & the Rokkets' garage rock'n'roll, plus late-80s beat/ska bands that grew out of it — only the Beat Takeshi ballad sits apart. a_recs offers polished J-pop ballads and 90s mainstream rock with no stylistic link to the seed's grit.

Both lists stay in the honky-tonk/roots world the seed lives in. a_recs is five more Arty Hill cuts — all stylistically right, including a live take that adds little — but tells a listener nothing they don't already have. b_recs keeps the twangy honky-tonk core with Hill's own band and Bill Kirchen's Telecaster shuffle, adds Billy Joe Shaver's outlaw grit, and only loosens with Pete Bernhard's darker solo acoustic blues, which is roots-adjacent but a different mood. Better spread, comparable fit.

The seed is a sparse, aching piano-led Korean drama OST ballad. a_recs is consistently in that world: Jung Seung Hwan and Heize's OST ballads, Kim Feel's soft indie-folk, Baek Yerin's melancholic indie-pop, plus another Sondia track in the same hushed register — varied but tightly on-mood. b_recs only lands with the second Sondia song; a live IU cut is looser, 015B is 90s synth-pop from a different era and production world, and two picks I can't place leave the list thin and unreliable.

Cruel Force is raw German blackened speed metal in the Bathory/Venom mould. b_recs lands exactly there: Diabolic Night, Hellripper, Midnight and Desaster are the same black/speed/thrash underground with the same filthy production, plus one more Cruel Force cut that fits. a_recs offers polished melodic death (In Flames, Insomnium), modern deathcore, and then psych-pop and future funk, which have no relationship to the seed at all.

VASSLINE is Korean metallic hardcore with death-metal edges and thick, heavy production. Slant sit in the same Seoul hardcore scene but play raw, short, D-beat-driven hardcore punk — adjacent community, noticeably lighter and rawer sound, so acceptable rather than close. The Vassline picks are from the seed's own metallic-hardcore body of work and match tone, riffing and production exactly. Both lists are single-artist and equally thin on discovery, so the tighter sonic match decides it.

The seed is the classic Hebrew folk/Israeli-song repertoire in a gentle vocal arrangement. a_recs stays squarely in that world: another traditional zemer by the same ensemble, the iconic 'Yerushalayim Shel Zahav', and a Ladino traditional piece, plus a modern Israeli devotional song that is a looser but plausible neighbour. b_recs offers five English-titled tracks credited to 'Shir' that I cannot place at all; they read as an artist-name collision rather than the same Hebrew-song tradition, so the list gives a listener nothing verifiable to go on.

Seed is Jun Togawa's Yapoos: theatrical 80s Japanese new wave/avant-pop. List a nails it with two Yapoos cuts from the same period and Hikashu, a peer from exactly that techno/new-wave scene; Kiyoshiro is adjacent Japanese rock, and only the Hamada ballad is plainly wrong. List b gets Togawa's own solo material right, but Akina Nakamori, an enka standard and Kai Band share only the era and language, not the sound. a is both more accurate and opens onto the wider scene.
I do not know EmptyORio or this track well enough to describe its sound, so I cannot judge whether the Taiwanese indie-rock picks or the Taiyu/Mandopop picks are the closer match.
I do not know 熱寫生 or this track well enough to characterise its genre, era or production, so I cannot judge how closely either list matches it.

The seed is a soft Mandopop ballad from Singapore's 90s scene. a_recs lands squarely there: Mavis Hee is essentially the same vocal-ballad territory, Cass Phang brings the parallel HK ballad sound, Joi Chua and Stefanie Sun extend it into the slightly later Singaporean wave, and the Kit Chan track itself fits the mood. b_recs consists of obscure online covers, improvisations and marginal network-pop entries that I cannot place with confidence; nothing there reads as a considered ballad match.

The seed sits in the older Cantonese operatic/festive-song world. Both lists open with the same well-matched 文千岁 track, but a_recs then drifts into 80s Cantopop ballads, a TV theme and an English-language Wynners pop song, which share little with the seed's vintage vocal style. b_recs stays with older festive and traditional-leaning Chinese vocal repertoire (贺年歌-style pieces, a 徐小凤 live cut, another 香港靓女多 reading), giving a far more coherent 'more like this' set, even if the live track is a slight mismatch.

The seed is Afterlife-flavoured melodic house/indie dance with warm organic production. a_recs stays in that lane throughout — RÜFÜS DU SOL's own material, Elderbrook, Hayden James and Panama all share the vocal-led, mid-tempo, emotive character; the Adriatique version is essentially another mix of the seed song, so it fits sonically but adds little. b_recs has two very strong picks (RÜFÜS DU SOL, Adriatique) but pairs them with big-room Armin van Buuren trance, which is a different scene and energy entirely, and one track I can't place. a_recs is the more coherent and usable set.

Baaba Maal's Traveller sits in modern West African song with atmospheric, electronic-tinged production. b_recs stays inside that world: Youssou N'Dour is the closest possible Senegalese peer, Mabandla brings the contemporary Afro-folk angle, Mtukudzi and Rajery widen the map without leaving the family, and a same-album Baaba Maal track fits naturally. a_recs wanders into indie rock, vintage jazz and 70s singer-songwriter material with no stylistic link; only Moses Sumney shares any atmospheric kinship.

The seed is an early-80s TVB-style sentimental Cantonese ballad. b_recs sits squarely in that world: 倆忘煙水裡 and 不裝飾你的夢 are exactly the same era, arrangement and mood, with a same-artist ballad and a Paula Tsui track (only weakened by being a Mandarin live cut). a_recs has good period picks in 問我 and 似是故人來, but 餓狼傳說 is a mid-90s uptempo dance number that breaks the mood badly, and the Kenny Bee track is a later, brighter ballad.

The seed is a 1979 Taiwanese campus-folk staple: gentle acoustic guitar, nostalgic and warm. b_recs lands squarely in that world — 童年 and 葉佳修's 赤足走在田埂上 (by the seed's own composer) are near-perfect companions, plus another Pan An-bang track and two adjacent Mandarin easy-listening ballads. a_recs re-serves the query song itself, which is worthless to the listener, and pads with mainland 80s material (喀秋莎, 军港之夜) that shares little beyond gentleness. Only 年輕人的心聲 truly fits there.

Darkest Horizon play modern, technically polished melodic death metal, so their own catalogue tracks are inherently a tight sonic match — but five of them is a thin 'more like this' result for someone already playing the band. b_recs lands the same territory across the scene: Mors Principium Est and The Halo Effect are near-perfect melodeath matches, with Children of Bodom, Whispered and Engel sitting slightly to the side in keyboard-led, symphonic and modern-groove directions. That list is far more useful.

The seed sits in the Taiwanese instrumental post-rock/math-rock world, and a_recs maps that scene well: Donkey's Ears, TFAP and Paint The Sky Red share the twinkly guitar-layering and slow-build dynamics, Themilo is a slightly dreamier Thai cousin, and the same-artist cut is a natural companion. b_recs is four more Pleiades tracks — all fitting, but a listener already there learns nothing — capped off by a Japanese idol-group intro that has no sonic relationship at all. a_recs is the more useful result.

EXID's 'Up & Down' is mid-2010s girl-group pop with a brassy, sultry hook. a_recs lands the closest neighbours: Girl's Day's 'Something' shares almost the same year and sexy-retro production, and the 4minute/miss A picks keep the attitude even if they're a few years earlier; only Apink's bright 'Alright' drifts. b_recs has the single best match in Stellar's 'Marionette' and digs up Badkiz, but Apink's 'NoNoNo' and 2NE1's electro-hip-hop swagger sit further from the seed's groove. Slight edge to a on overall closeness, b for discovery.

The seed is an early-90s Taiwanese Mandarin ballad from the Rock Records/李宗盛 circle. b_recs lands squarely there: 陳淑樺's 夢醒時分 shares the same writer and era, 大雨 is a stylistic sibling by the same singer, 孟庭葦 continues the early-90s female ballad line, and 鳳飛飛/木吉他 fill in the Taiwanese pop-folk lineage behind it. a_recs drifts into mainland 90s/2000s pop and network songs, with 鳳凰傳奇's ethnic dance-pop plainly out of place and 徐小鳳's Live standard from a different vintage.

Kirakiraboshi is hazy, loop-based Japanese ambient from Sakura. b_recs stays in that world: another Sakura piece, Meitei's dusty Japanese ambient, and Biosphere's cool minimal ambient are all strong matches, with Mort Garson a mild era outlier. a_recs only truly connects via the Yokota track credited in kanji; Kid Koala's turntablist cut-ups and a bright anime BGM cue pull away from the seed's drifting mood, and two picks I can't place leave the list thin.

The seed is a straightforward Namo Amitabha devotional chant. a_recs stays entirely inside that world: another chant by the same singer, a temple choir's Medicine Buddha recitation, Imee Ooi's Diamond Sutra, and Guanyin devotional songs — same solemn, repetitive, chant-led character, with some spread across styles from pure recitation to melodic Buddhist pop. b_recs has one strong chant match (印能法师) but surrounds it with mainland pop remixes and unrelated electronic/dance material that share nothing with the seed's devotional purpose or sonic texture.

The seed is Andean charango instrumental folk. b_recs is five more Cavour pieces, all squarely in the same charango idiom and flawless on fit, but a listener who just played Cavour gains little from a list that never leaves him. a_recs keeps the charango core (another Cavour track, a Bolivian charango player, Los Calchakis' Andean folk) while opening the scene wider; only the Violeta Parra vocal drifts toward nueva canción, and one candidate I can't place.

elijah woods works in bright, hooky bedroom/indie-pop with clean synth-pop production. a_recs stays in that lane: his own similarly styled track, gavn! and vaultboy are close scene matches, with Zach Seabaugh and Zack Tabudlo drifting toward softer singer-songwriter ballad territory. In b_recs only Finding Hope is placeable for me — a lo-fi sad-pop cousin rather than a match — and the remaining four artists I cannot situate at all, so the list offers little I can vouch for.

The seed is mid-80s Japanese idol pop with a city-pop sheen. B lands squarely in that world: Yoshimoto Miyoko and Kudo Yuki are contemporaneous idol singles, Kokubu Yurie brings the AOR/city-pop side, and Ohtaki is the adjacent Niagara production lineage; the same-artist track also fits stylistically. A wanders across decades and styles — 70s folk rock, a 90s Komuro dance hit, an enka-leaning ballad — with only Kisugi Takao coming near the era and mood.

Dakis sits in 60s/70s Greek light pop (elafrolaiko, beat-era covers). A mixes one solid same-era pick (Voskopoulos) and a Dakis track with clearly off-scene choices: Malamas is entehno folk, Konstantina is 90s laiko, Rena Morfi is contemporary. B stays inside the right era and vocal-pop sound throughout, though it leans heavily on Dakis himself and the Hatzinasios entry looks like an orchestral take on the seed song, which adds nothing. Still the more listenable continuation.

The seed is a Komuro Tetsuya-style J-pop power ballad re-recording. b_recs lands squarely in that world: globe and hitomi are the same Komuro/avex production lineage, Kahala's own DEPARTURES cover is a direct match, SPEED and GLAY are era- and scene-adjacent 90s J-pop. a_recs offers a children's folk standard, hyperpop and unrelated dance tracks; only Pandora's Eurodance has even a faint link to the Komuro sound's eurobeat leanings.

Seed is Chengdu dialect trap. a_recs stays largely inside that scene — 謝帝 and AnsrJ are core Sichuan-dialect rap, Pissy is adjacent (though a live cut), with 那奇沃夫 the loosest fit as a mainstream trap pick. b_recs has an excellent Asen pick and two more DDG tracks that fit, but 法老's Beijing style sits apart and two same-artist slots make the list thinner. a_recs opens more of the surrounding scene while keeping the dialect-rap character.

Para Bárbara is intimate Cuban nueva trova: solo guitar, dense poetic lyric. List a stays exactly there — Feliú's own guitar-and-voice songs plus Noel Nicola and Vicente Feliú, contemporaries from the same Havana trova circle, so it both fits and points the listener somewhere new. List b starts well with another Feliú and reasonable cantautor picks in Aute and Milanés, but Chavela Vargas's ranchera drama and Cabral's folk-philosophy are a different tradition and break the mood.

The seed is the Finlandia hymn as a serene sacred choral piece. A stays in that world: Fauré's Sanctus and Sibelius's own Rakastava are near-perfect matches, Elgar's part-songs and Mahler's 'Aufersteh'n' chorus keep the reverent choral mood, with only the solo-piano Impromptu drifting. B offers only composer continuity — violin salon pieces, a piano étude and two different recordings of the same Violin Concerto movement, all instrumental, virtuosic or restless rather than hymn-like, and the doubled concerto makes the list thinner still.

a_recs is five more Hillbilly Rawhide cuts: they obviously match the band's rockabilly/psychobilly punk sound, but a listener who just played the seed already has the album. b_recs keeps one on-point HR track and reaches into the same Brazilian booze-and-boots rock circle — Matanza's outlaw country-metal is a near-ideal neighbour, Velhas Virgens and Confraria da Costa are plausible if tamer, and only Ludov's indie rock is off-scene. That makes it the more useful 'more like this' list despite the weaker tail.
I do not know BG8LOCC or the track 'Uncrowned' well enough to characterise its sound, and most candidates on both sides are also unfamiliar to me, so I cannot judge fit honestly.

The seed is the classic Marathi Ganpati aarti in a traditional devotional arrangement. List a keeps the Marathi frame and includes a genuine Ganesh bhakti track (He Gajaanan Baba), with the rest being Sathe's Marathi light/bhavgeet material — adjacent but less ritual — spoiled by the Alisha Chinai pop track, which is wholly out of place. List b drifts toward Hindi bhajan and a Bollywood film song (Woh Kisna Hai), which shares only a broad devotional flavour, and several picks are too obscure to place. a is the more usable set.

The seed is a traditional East Asian instrumental ensemble piece. List b stays entirely inside that world — the same ensemble, plus Chinese traditional ensemble and classical instrumental pieces; the nationality shifts from Korean to Chinese but the acoustic instrumentation, tempo and serene mood carry over well. List a jumps to British pop balladry, an EDM bass track and a novelty cover, none of which share instrumentation, era or mood with the seed; a couple of the smaller-name tracks I can't place at all.

Stompin' Bird sits in the Japanese melodic hardcore/skate-punk circuit, and a_recs lands squarely there: Over Arm Throw, HOTSQUALL, locofrank and Boobie Trap share the same fast, melodic, English-shouted attack and label-scene sound. b_recs is scattered — STANCE PUNKS and Hump Back are at least punk-adjacent, The 50 Kaitenz is garage rock'n'roll, and two acoustic folk tracks by Humbert Humbert have nothing to do with the seed's energy or production.

I do not know Itoko Toma's music well enough to describe the sound of this track, so I cannot judge which recommendations sit close to it. Rating the candidates would mean guessing from titles and playlist associations rather than from the seed's actual style.

LINION's smooth Taiwanese neo-soul/bedroom R&B is best matched by his own material and by Osean, whose soul-pop sits in the same scene — a_recs delivers both, though Karen Mok and Eric Chou pull toward mainstream Mandopop ballads. b_recs has one strong LINION track but the rest are mainland internet-pop ballads, a very different production world from the seed's warm live-band R&B, and largely unplaceable. a_recs is the more usable list.

Stilz sits in the driving outrun corner of synthwave, and a_recs stays right there: VHS Dreams, NightStop and Absolute Valentine share the same pulsing arpeggios and neon-highway production, with Timecop1983 only slightly softer. b_recs is all credible synthwave but drifts further out — Perturbator is heavier darksynth, Mitch Murder is cleaner retro pastiche, and Jasper Byrne's Hotline Miami material is murkier and more ambient than Stilz's polished outrun. Both lists spread across artists; a's centre of gravity matches the seed better.

The seed is functional yoga/ambient instrumental music built around breath pacing. B stays inside that exact lane throughout — soft ambient beds, gentle guitar, nothing that breaks the flow — even though three picks are from the seed artist itself. A drifts toward devotional mantra chanting and plain nature-sound recordings, which serve a different purpose than a flowing instrumental yoga track, and one candidate I cannot place. B is the safer continuous listen; A opens more catalogue but at the cost of mood consistency.

The seed is a soft acoustic cover of a pop ballad, the kind of hushed guitar/piano reworking that lives on chill-acoustic playlists. B stays squarely in that lane: acoustic covers of familiar pop hits by small cover acts, same intimate arrangements and production, including a companion track by the same artist. A drifts into contemporary R&B (Tinashe, Giveon) and jazz-standard vocal territory, which shares only a general 'mellow' feel; the tone, rhythm and production are noticeably different, and a couple of picks I cannot place.

Both lists stay in the German maritime-song world. B is tightly on target — a Carolinensiel shanty-choir potpourri plus three more Frische Brise tracks — but three of five are the seed's own choir, so it opens little up. A offers genuine peers from other shanty and navy choirs (Blaue Jungs, Baltrum) alongside the seed artist, and its looser picks (Santiano's folk-rock, Curd Jürgens' Reeperbahn schlager) still share the seafaring theme even though the production is quite different. Broader and more useful.
I do not know Shennumbanine or this track well enough to describe its sound, so I cannot judge how closely any of the candidates match its scene, era or production character.

"Axe Crazy" is fast, raw NWOBHM. The b list stays exactly in that world: another Jaguar cut from the same period, plus Hollow Ground, Girlschool, Tysondog and Ostrogoth — all early-80s British/European speed-edged metal with the same rough production, and it broadens the listener's horizon. The a list is entirely Jaguar's own catalogue; the tracks are stylistically close enough, but several are the band's more mid-paced rock material, one credit appears to point at an unrelated act, and the list adds nothing beyond the band the listener already has.

a_recs keeps the Tuvan/Mongolian throat-singing world intact: Alash Ensemble is the closest possible sibling, Yat-Kha is Tuvan with a rockier edge, and Egschiglen/Altai Khangai bring the neighbouring Mongolian ensemble sound. b_recs is four more Huun-Huur-Tu tracks — all perfectly on-style but adding nothing a listener of the seed doesn't already have — plus a Chinese solo piano piece that has no connection to igil, khoomei or the steppe idiom at all. a_recs is the more useful discovery set.

Kane's world is sparse, groove-driven acoustic Americana. a_recs nails the immediate circle — Kevin Welch and Rayna Gellert are his own Dead Reckoning/duo collaborators, and the Kane cuts sit right beside the seed — but three of five slots are Kane himself plus two live takes, so it barely moves past what the listener already has. b_recs keeps one Kane track and then reaches into Gurf Morlix and Neal Casal, both close in tone; Old 97's and Lucero are rowdier and rockier than Kane's understated feel, but the list as a whole is the more useful 'more like this'.

250's track is a moody, retro-leaning Korean electronic piece rooted in ppong/synth textures. a_recs drifts into electro-swing and French nu-disco, which share only a vintage-sample surface, and the Bad Omens metalcore pick is completely unrelated; only the other 250 cut belongs. b_recs opens with the seed itself, which is worthless as a recommendation, but XXX and Clazziquai sit in the same Korean alt-electronic/label ecosystem and mood, making the rest of the list far more usable despite two tracks I can't place.

Both lists stay inside the Iranian alternative/fusion world the seed belongs to. List a is mostly the seed's own catalogue plus what appears to be the same song 'Darya/دریا' credited twice, which tells a listener nothing new. List b keeps one Niaz Nawab track and otherwise reaches across the same Tehran alt/indie scene — Pallett, Namjoo, Radio Tehran — with only the glossier Rana Mansour pop track drifting off style, so it is the more useful 'more like this' result.

The seed is scrappy Beijing garage/punk rock with lo-fi guitars and sardonic vocals. b_recs stays right in that world: another 脏手指 cut, Joyside's punk, 假假條's noisy art-rock and 回春丹's indie rock, with only 郭顶's polished dream-pop drifting softer. a_recs offers 80s Cantopop and hip-hop/R&B adjacent tracks with no guitar-band link at all; several I can't place, and the ones I can are far off. b_recs is both the better fit and the more useful map of the scene.

The seed is Taiwanese guitar rock with an emotive, band-driven sound. a_recs stays inside that world: Mary See the Future and Hello Nico are core Taiwanese indie rock, 脫拉庫 shares the older Taiwan band-scene energy, 甜約翰 is softer but still indie band territory, and the same-artist track fits naturally. b_recs is scattered — mandopop ballad, mainland folk-pop, and Shanghai dialect novelty rock share little with the seed beyond language; only the 四分衛 cut and THE 尺口MP land near the target.

Robine sits in the acoustic chanson/folk revival with a strong libertarian, chanson-à-texte streak. List a lands exactly there: Vian's antimilitarist classic, an anarchist song, Ogeret's traditional repertoire, and Yacoub's Malicorne-rooted folk — same guitar-and-voice, text-driven world, and it spreads across several artists rather than looping back to Robine only. List b is yé-yé pop, a film-score instrumental and modern indie pop; only Emily Loizeau shares any chanson kinship, and even she is a different era and production entirely.

Both lists stay in the same warm, vocal-tinged deep house lane as "Bella". A is tightly on-target but is essentially the Finnebassen catalogue plus remixes of his own tracks — a listener who just played him gains little. B keeps one strong Finnebassen cut and surrounds it with scene-adjacent deep/tech house from Miguel Campbell and Karmon, which is a more useful "more like this" result even if one pick is slightly cooler and more club-techno in character.

The seed is Kenji Kawai's Ghost in the Shell chant rebuilt as a big, brash Steve Aoki club track, so the useful neighbours are festival EDM and remix culture. The a list stays in that world — big-room, hard dance and a drum'n'bass remix — even if none matches the cinematic chant element exactly. The b list is Japanese doujin/Touhou vocal arrange material plus a 90s folk-rock band; the only real link is Japanese origin, and たま in particular has nothing to do with the seed's production character.

Møme's Aloha is sunny French tropical/chill house with warm synths and breezy vocals. B lands squarely in that scene — Tez Cadey, Petit Biscuit and Feder are the exact French melodic-house peers, plus a well-chosen Møme track from the same sonic world. A drifts: Rhye and DEAMN are at least chilled electronic-adjacent, but the Cannons cover is indie synth-pop, while Ash Code's darkwave and Camera Obscura's twee indie pop have no relationship to the seed at all.

ABC's lush 1982 synth-pop sits squarely in the British new-romantic/sophisti-pop world, and a_recs stays there: Kajagoogoo, Frankie Goes to Hollywood and Nik Kershaw are era-perfect, ABC's own later single fits, and Pet Shop Boys is only a decade off in production. b_recs offers contemporary rap and R&B with no stylistic, era or production link to the seed.

The seed is 1930s-40s Shanghai shidaiqu. Both lists anchor correctly with Zhou Xuan and peers, but a_recs drifts badly at the end: Xie Lei is Taiwanese oldies decades later and Tian Zhen is 90s mainland pop-rock, wholly unrelated to the crackly big-band cabaret sound. b_recs has one intruder (Hu Defu's 70s campus folk) but otherwise stays inside the era with Wu Yingyin, Zhou Xuan and two more Bai Hong sides that match the seed's orchestration and vocal style.

The seed sits in the instrumental lofi hip-hop / chillhop world — dusty drums, jazzy chords, mellow tempo — and both lists stay squarely inside that scene. a_recs pairs a companion track by the same producer with peers like [bsd.u] and Cotard Beatz; b_recs spreads across five different beatmakers, with j'san and GRILLABEATS being especially natural neighbours. Neither list wanders off-genre, and neither offers a clear advantage in depth or discovery, so this is a genuine draw.

The seed is an intimate solo-piano miniature on Armenian folk themes. b_recs stays in that world: more Ayrapetyan piano arrangements of Armenian/spiritual material fit perfectly, and the Buniatishvili tracks are at least solo piano recital repertoire, though Scarlatti and the Gainsbourg arrangement drift away in era and character. a_recs offers contemporary pop, rap and electronic tracks with no connection at all to solo classical piano — a listener would be jolted out of the mood immediately.

Field Mob's "So What" is early-2000s Dirty South rap with a bouncy, radio-friendly hook. b_recs sits in that world: Lil' Flip's "Sunshine" is near-perfect, Chingy is the same crossover Southern rap lane, with Ciara and Kelly Rowland drifting into mid-2000s R&B and Salt-N-Pepa a decade off. a_recs offers Men I Trust's dream pop and Melanie Martinez's alt-pop, which have nothing to do with the seed, plus several tracks too obscure to place.
I cannot place SADOG's sound reliably, and nearly all candidate artists in both lists are outside my knowledge, so any scoring would be guesswork based on naming style rather than music.

The seed is melodic Chinese trap/R&B from the Rap of China circle. a_recs lands squarely in that scene: another 李佳隆 cut, plus GALI and 艾熱 whose auto-tuned melodic trap shares the same production sheen, and 黃旭's rap take on 說散就散 fits the sentimental-hip-hop mood. b_recs opens with a Japanese pop novelty track that has no connection at all, and the rest are obscure or look like reuploads/covers, offering little a listener could use.

The seed is polished 7SENSES idol dance-pop from the SNH48 family. a_recs leads with another 7SENSES track and the parent group, then widens sensibly into C-pop idol acts with comparable production, so the sonic character stays close. b_recs stays inside the SNH48 orbit but leans on individual members' solo cuts and a live stage recording, which are patchier in production and mood than the seed's sleek single sound, and the live take is a weaker 'next track' choice.

Vincy Chan's ballad sits in mid-2000s/2010s EEG-era Cantopop. List a stays right in that world: her own track, Sherman Chung and Mag Lam are direct stylistic peers, with Sammi Cheng and a Leo Ku live cut only slightly off in era or format. List b drifts — Freya Lim is Taiwanese Mandarin ballad territory, and Steven Ma's late-90s TVB-drama ballads are a thinner, older sound; only Jade Kwan is a close match, and one entry I can't place.

The seed is Yukadan's gritty Osaka blues with Kimura's raw vocal. a_recs is entirely Yukadan's Gegege no Kitaro project material — skits and character pieces tied to the cartoon rather than the band's blues songs, so despite the artist match it delivers almost none of the seed's sound and no variety at all. b_recs leads with a genuine Yukadan blues number and then branches into the adjacent Kansai folk/singer-songwriter world (Folk Crusaders, Old Days Tailor, Shimoda) plus BEGIN's bluesy pop — looser fits, but the list is usable and opens things up.

The seed is contemporary Afrikaans sokkie/country-pop. List a is five more Lianie May tracks: all stylistically on target, but a listener who just played her already knows her catalogue, so the list adds little. List b keeps one Lianie May cut and reaches into the same Afrikaans sokkie/pop scene with Brendan Peyper, which is an ideal match, plus Jo Black's more singer-songwriter ballad style as a looser fit. b opens up the scene without leaving it.

The seed is early-80s American jangle/power pop from the Mitch Easter school. a_recs lands squarely there: skinny-tie power pop (The Records), Athens-scene guitar jangle (Love Tractor), Hitchcock's chiming psych-pop, plus a later power-pop descendant in Sloan, and a same-band track that genuinely matches. b_recs wanders into synthpop, hi-NRG, Celtic folk-punk and Taiwanese math rock — no shared guitar sound, scene or production character with the query.

Sinmara's dense, dissonant Icelandic black metal is served well by both lists sonically. a_recs is five more Sinmara cuts — all fitting, including earlier harsher Aphotic Womb material, but it tells a listener nothing they don't already have. b_recs keeps one Sinmara track and opens into the exact same Reykjavík circle (Almyrkvi, Svartidauði, Skáphe), with Mgła as a slightly cleaner, more melodic outlier that still sits in the same modern black metal world.

Both lists stay in Catie Curtis's warm acoustic singer-songwriter territory. a_recs pairs one of her own tracks with Deb Talan and Antje Duvekot, who share the same intimate contemporary-folk voice-and-guitar sound, plus Americana-leaning Gretchen Peters and the more retro-harmony Secret Sisters, which drifts slightly. b_recs is five more of her own songs — they fit, but include a Bacharach cover and a quirkier novelty cut, and the list tells a listener nothing new. a_recs is the more useful 'more like this'.

Suyano sits in the Dutch festival-EDM lane (big room / future-house, Revealed/Hexagon-style). In list a, another Suyano cut and Kill The Buzz land squarely there, but Sultan + Shepard's deep progressive house is a noticeably calmer, more introspective sound than a bright festival record, and two picks I can't place. List b's Manse, Arston and WildVibes all live in that same melodic festival/future-house ecosystem with comparable energy and production gloss, giving a more consistent set without relying on the seed artist. Several unknowns on both sides keep confidence low.

Garion is old-school Korean boombap with dense Korean-language flows. In a_recs, Infinite Flow sits in the same underground scene, while Junoflo and Primary are much later, glossier hip hop and Jaurim's alt-rock is simply off-genre. b_recs stays inside Korean rap: Garion's own 'Post Mortem' matches the sound exactly and YDG is era-appropriate, though PSY's intro and Outsider's melodic speed-rap are pop-leaning misses. b holds the tighter scene overall despite less discovery value.

I do not know Effie or this track well enough to describe its sound, so I cannot judge whether the underground/hyperpop-leaning candidates in either list actually match its genre, era or production character.

The seed is Sandee Chan's arty, electronically-tinged Mandarin indie pop. Both lists anchor with another Sandee Chan track, which fits. A then adds 自然卷, a genuine Taiwanese indie neighbour, but falls apart with a mainland trap rap track and an ACG/古風 vocalist that share nothing with the seed. B stays in the Taiwanese alt-pop orbit — Faith Yang is a near-perfect stylistic sibling — and its weak picks are merely bland mainstream ballads rather than outright mismatches, making it the safer, more coherent list.

Labios rotos is spacey Mexican alt-rock, and list A lands squarely in that scene: Enjambre and San Pascualito Rey are peers, Zoé's own 'Soñé' is a direct match, León Larregui is the same voice solo, and La Castañeda is a slightly darker 90s cousin. List B looks to have collided with unrelated artists sharing the name — a techno track featuring a different Zøe is plainly wrong, and the remaining picks I can't place in this scene at all, leaving only a live bolero cover as plausible.

小半 is soft mainland indie-folk/pop with intimate female vocals. a_recs stays inside that world: another 陈粒 track, 宋冬野's 斑马斑马 is the canonical neighbour, 阿肆 is close indie-pop, 老狼 is older campus folk but same family. b_recs has plausible soft singer-songwriter picks in 郑润泽 (though doubled), but drops in 人間椅子, a Japanese heavy prog-metal band, which is jarringly wrong and spoils the set; two other entries are too obscure to place.

I don't know Pay4n or this track, and cannot place its genre, era or production character, so I cannot judge how well any of the candidates would follow it. Most of the recommended artists are also unfamiliar to me, so any rating would be guesswork based on names alone.

Lujiachi works in Taipei's experimental/hard-drum club world, so every a_recs entry sits exactly in that sonic space — but it is four of his own tracks plus his own remix, which tells a listener nothing they couldn't find on his page. b_recs reaches into the same scene properly: Meuko! Meuko! is an almost ideal neighbour, Scintii and Triodust share the deconstructed-club and Eastern Margins aesthetic. Lifeformed's Dustforce chiptune-ambient cue is badly out of place, but the list still opens the scene up.

The seed is Chinese-language indie rock with guitar-led band arrangements. a_recs stays in that Sinophone indie orbit — Schoolgirl Byebye's dream-pop is close in scene, another Hertz track anchors it, and Yoyo Sham is softer but still HK indie songwriting. b_recs' three extra Hertz tracks fit well but add little a listener doesn't already know, and the conservatory choral setting of 沁园春·长沙 is completely outside the scene, which spoils the list. Several candidates on both sides I could not place.

a_recs is five more Dead Kennedys cuts, mostly Plastic Surgery Disasters — all genuinely sonically right, but a listener who just played Holiday in Cambodia already has this record. b_recs keeps one perfect same-session pick (Police Truck) and then opens out into the wider early-80s American punk world: Agent Orange's Californian surf-punk grit, The Dickies' fast LA snottiness, Minor Threat's DC hardcore, and Geza X, whose sound is directly tied to the Fresh Fruit sessions. Same scene, era and intensity, with far more discovery value.

Cryfemal's raw, aggressive one-man black metal is served perfectly by b_recs — every cut shares the same lo-fi buzz and Spanish necro atmosphere — but it is five tracks from the same project, which tells a listener nothing new. a_recs keeps one Cryfemal track and reaches into the wider raw/underground black metal world: Dodsferd is a strong stylistic match, while Xasthur, Despondent Moon and Trhä drift toward depressive or atmospheric territory that is looser in intensity but still the same family, and the list is far more useful.

ダウト play showa-flavoured, energetic visual kei. a_recs stays inside that world: another Dauto track, vistlip and DIAURA from the same modern VK scene, Megamasso's retro-pop cover matching the kayokyoku streak, with MIYAVI a slightly looser solo-rock pick. b_recs opens well with D and DaizyStripper, but then drops into idol pop (AKB48, Watanabe Miyuki) and a novelty act, which share nothing with the seed's guitar-driven VK sound.

The seed is a gentle piano-led Mandopop breakup ballad. a_recs stays squarely in that lane: another Victor Wong ballad plus Rachel Liang, Lin Fan, Lin Yu Zhong and Aska Yang, all same-era mid-tempo Mandarin ballads with similar vocal warmth, and it spreads across several artists. b_recs has two ideal picks in Michael Wong, the seed singer's own duo partner and stylistic twin, but the other three are obscure acts I can't place, leaving the list half unusable in practice.

The seed is a Marathi abhang/bhajan in the warhkari devotional idiom. Both lists stay largely in Marathi bhakti-geet territory: Hiremath's abhangs and the Shubhangi Joshi aarti/abhang tracks all sit close to the seed's mood and instrumentation. b_recs includes the strongest single match (Avaghe Garaje Pandharpur) but is diluted by Jaanta Raja, a Shivaji-themed folk/powada piece with a very different character, and a Hindi Hanuman aarti. a_recs holds the devotional register throughout, though the Krishna bhajan in Hindi drifts slightly.

The seed is Karaindrou's chamber-melancholic Angelopoulos score: accordion, strings, modal Greek laments. List a keeps that world and widens it usefully — another Karaindrou piece, Reboutsika's Greek film melodicism, and Preisner's Kieslowski writing, which is almost a sibling aesthetic; the Persian violin and solo-piano picks are looser but still slow, sorrowful instrumentals. List b's three Karaindrou tracks are perfect matches but tell a listener nothing new, and Woodkid's brass-driven orchestral pop and Badalamenti's noir-synth mood sit further from the acoustic chamber sound. a is the more useful handful.

The seed sits in the Japanese screamo/emoviolence scene, and a_recs maps that world precisely: sassya-, killie, moreru and くだらない1日 all share the frantic tempos, raw production and shouted vocals; only Ling tosite sigure drifts toward cleaner mainstream math-rock. b_recs is four more lang tracks — stylistically safe but nothing a listener doesn't already have access to — plus Lang Elliott, a nature-recording artist matched purely on name, which is a jarring miss.

The seed is a Carinthian dialect male-quartet Volkslied. All of a_recs is the same group singing the same repertoire — flawless sonic fit, but it tells a listener nothing they don't already have. b_recs keeps one Kärntner Viergesang track and adds Montanara Chor, a larger alpine male choir with the same warm unaccompanied German folk-song character; slightly bigger, more German-standard repertoire than Carinthian dialect, and the Beethoven sacred piece drifts toward the concert hall. Still the more useful 'more like this' result.

The seed is acoustic Japanese jazz piano. a_recs stays in that world: another Yamanaka piano arrangement plus Japanese jazz/fusion players (Terai's violin, Matsumoto's tenor standards), with Casiopea's electric fusion the loosest link. b_recs has two strong Yamanaka piano tracks, but Yamashita's doo-wop a cappella standard is stylistically off and the enormous yacht-rock DJ megamix is unusable as a next track. a_recs is the more coherent and more exploratory list.

Selvageria is heavy Brazilian metallic hardcore/thrash. a_recs starts well with another Selvageria track and Desalmado's grinding Brazilian extremity is at least adjacent, but Impurity's raw black metal sits in a different scene and MegaDriver's video-game metal instrumental covers are plainly wrong for a hardcore listener. b_recs is entirely the seed band, which opens nothing up and is a thin result, yet every track genuinely matches the sound and tempo. The absence of any misfire makes b the list I would rather be handed.

Kawa's sound is Yunnan Wa ethnic folk crossed with reggae/ska and party-style drinking songs. b_recs stays in that world: another Kawa track, Hanggai's Mongolian folk-rock drinking song, and Li Naluo's Yunnan ethnic folk are all natural neighbours. a_recs pairs one strong same-artist drinking song with two Xie Tianxiao grunge/psych-rock tracks, which are a different intensity and instrumentation entirely; the Taiwanese ska pick is closer but from another scene. Several candidates in both lists I cannot place.

"Heart Attack" is loud, belted 2013 radio pop with pop-rock guitars. List b sits squarely in that world: Demi's own contemporaneous single, Taylor Swift's 2012 crossover, plus adjacent teen-pop and pop-punk names that share the vocal-forward, chorus-driven build, even if a couple lean smoother or later. List a drifts far off: an acoustic cut, a Chinese game OST, and obscure dance-pop with little stylistic link; only The Cab lands in a related pop-rock zone, and as a ballad it misses the energy.

Both lists stay inside German-language black metal. b_recs is five more Totenwache tracks: all fit the seed's raw German black metal sound perfectly, but a listener who just played one already has the discography and learns nothing new. a_recs keeps the same scene through Mavorim and Runenwacht, with Non Est Deus and Dark Fortress drifting toward industrial and melodic/avant-garde territory — a slightly looser fit, but a far more useful 'more like this' result.

譚炳文 sits in the early Cantonese pop / oldies world with opera-tinged phrasing. A's two 任劍輝 pieces are genuine Cantonese opera classics — culturally adjacent heritage listening, but a different form from a crooned pop song, and the 蔡琴/張學友/甄妮 picks jump to later Mandarin and 80s-90s Cantopop with no real link. B leads with 鄭錦昌's 新禪院鐘聲, almost the ideal match: same 60s-70s Cantonese oldies scene and delivery, and Frances Yip's standard plus 羅嘉良's retro-styled ballad stay loosely in that lane. 草蜢's dance-pop and 蘇永康 are misfires, but B's best pick is far stronger.
